Between each major materials meltdown, we turned to FDM (Fused Deposition Modeling) as our trusty “rapid sketch” tool.

It let us iterate on design tweaks quickly. Hardware is really slow and painful, so anything you can do to reduce the iteration cycle pays dividends massively.

1906056495814307949.text: Why block sparse? The standard transformer attention mechanism computes attention scores between all pairs of tokens in a sequence. which leads to O(n²) complexity in both computation and memory

1906056501719953468.text: BSBR addresses this scalability issue by breaking the sequence into chucks of block size B and then combining standard attention within fixed-size chunks and a meta-attention mechanism to efficiently retrieve information between chunks. It works by compressing each chunk’s…

1906056515192328598.text:
The chunk size (B) is a crucial hyperparameter that affects:
- Memory Usage: Larger chunks use more memory but provide better local context
- Computation Time: Smaller chunks are faster but may miss important long-range dependencies
- Model Expressivity: Chunk size affects how…

1906056522041582067.text: You can control the compression factor which determines how much information is preserved in chunk states. Higher compression factors reduce memory usage and speed up computation but may lose fine-grained information:

1906056529008079170.text: BSBR also supports overlap between chunks which may help mitigate attention discontinuities at the block boundaries:

1906056531834990820.text: And besides sparse attention, the implementation also supports state reuse across layers, optimized attention masks for autoregression, and I plan on implementing more streaming-first optimizations when I get time.
